title: Port from bookdown to quarto
description:
Substantive changes

- Converts code chunk options to yaml format
- Fixes issues with placement of level one headers
- Switches the github actions workflow to quarto
- Replaces _bookdown.yml and _output.yml with _quarto.yml
- Uses quarto layouts in place of `columns()` function (currently only fixes the number of columns, not the size or aspect ratio of plots)

Other changes

- Additional canonicalisation for files that escaped the last round
- .RProj file explicitly enforces sentence level wrapping of markdown
- Adds a `status()` function to show callouts for each chapter
- `set.seed()` called consistently in common.R instead of inconsistently in some chapters
- Fixes a couple of broken cross-references

Something confusing

- For reasons that I don't yet understand, I had to slightly change one heading in the springs chapter to prevent quarto from throwing errors. Reproducible locally and on actions, but as yet I haven't managed to isolate it as a minimal reprex: 81c4ae5f1af7b30abae2cb3c341b85e9026f7d9f

Proposed next steps

- PR to rename .Rmd files to .qmd (and rename scripts like common.R to _common.R etc)
- Then return to updating the actual content 😀

title: Updates internals and extensions chapters
description:
A first pass at smoothing the ggplot2 internals and extensions chapters: 

- For the internals chapter the changes are all in the ggproto section and are focused on extending the "Person" example (e.g., "Royalty" and "Police" both subclass "Person"). 
- I've made more extensive changes in the extensions chapter, providing small examples of each kind of ggplot2 extension (some of which are shamelessly stolen from vignettes, old issues threads, and in one case from ggforce) to illustrate the process. What I'm trying to do in each case is give novice developers a little more scaffolding, so that there aren't quite so many unfamiliar concepts once they hit the full "springs" case study in the final chapter (which I've not yet touched except in trivial ways).... but being a novice ggplot2 developer myself I'm not sure how well I've done it or what important points I've missed, and I think this is at the point where it needs suggestions from experts! 😀 

The other big PR in the pipeline at the moment is the scales toolbox edits (#260), and I've checked that this doesn't conflict with that one. I was thinking that since I've already dropped #260 on @hadley, and this is focused on chapters @thomasp85 has worked on, maybe Thomas could take a look at this and make suggestions?

title: Scales chapter
description:
First pass at the new scales chapter. The overall structure:

- The early sections are roughly the same: introduction then scale limits 
- Scale-specific sections are organised by aesthetic (position, colour, size, other) and then subdivided by fundamental type (continuous, discrete, binned)
- Transformations move to the end, making it easier to show transformations of non-position scales

Possible concerns:
 
- I *think* the merge conflicts are minor things, and hopefully remain so even after the guides PR is merged?
- Unsuprisingly, the colour scale section is long: there are so many continuous colour scales that I've subdivided (again!) into the general purpose scales (gradient, gradient2, gradientn) and the hand-picked palette scales (brewer/distiller, scico, paletteer). I think it works, but I don't love the fact that there are now level 4 headings.
- I still think there should be a section on transformations of binned scales, but at the moment I'm having troubles getting it to work. Either there is a bug, some unexpected behaviour, or I'm misunderstanding something. What I originally had in mind was to use binned scale transformations as an excuse to show how to define a novel transformation with the scales package, but obviously that's on hold while I figure out what's going on!
- My usual placeholder worry... I don't know what I don't know, so maybe I'm missing something important :upside_down_face: 

Other notes:

- There's a couple of places where the line length is suspiciously long (i.e., more than 80 chars). They do fit on one line when the book is rendered, but it's something I want to think about. Visually I don't want to break those cases over multiple lines if I can avoid it. 

In any case, I think it's reached the point where a review would help! :slightly_smiling_face:

title: Guides chapter
description:
First pass at a restructured and updated guides chapter. Notable changes in coverage:

- Covers the new `guide_*` functions (including the use of `guide_axis()` to rotate labels)
- Covers the new `draw_key_*` functions
- Updates the coverage of scales package (possibly needs more?)
- Briefly mentions `ggtext::element_markdown()` for formatted axis labels
- Briefly mentions `ggnewscale` package 

Stylistic changes:

- About half the examples use real data (`mpg` or `economics`)
- The "toy" examples are slightly modified allowing a single `toy` data frame to cover the whole chapter

Structural changes:

- Not a lot. Some reordering of content (guide functions appear earlier) but mostly it's modest

As usual, I haven't touched the exercises, and there's a lot of things I'm less than convinced of myself. However, I think it's at the point where a review would be the most effective way forward!

title: first pass at raster maps section
description:
This is a bare minimum pass at a raster maps section. 

I don't go into a lot of detail about the structure of a stars object, nor do I talk much about the different behaviour of `geom_stars` when `sf = TRUE` vs `sf = FALSE`. It does talk about the practicalities of obtaining data sets, plotting different sensor bands using `facet_wrap()`, overlaying vector maps on top of raster maps, and how to convert a more conventional data set into an sf geometry so that it can be transformed into the same CRS as the raster. 

There are a few minor things that annoy me: 

- originally I'd planned to use the infrared data image as well as the visible spectrum one, so there are two GeoTIFF files in the commit rather than one, but so far I haven't gotten around to doing anything interesting with it.
- the text refers to 14 images (which is what I pulled from the BOM server originally) but I've only committed two of them so the call to `list.files()` will presumably give the wrong answer.
- the code to download the data files relies on `purrr::walk2()` which feels like an unnecessary complication

Given the above I'm tempted to rewrite the download code to pretend I'd only ever downloaded one file instead of making the vectorised call to `curl::curl_download()`. Or two, if I find a use for the IR data! :slightly_smiling_face: 

It is definitely a work in progress, but I'm going to switch to other projects for the next couple of weeks so if you have a chance to take a look I'd appreciate feedback!

title: adding a running example to the internals chapter
description:
Not sure whether I'm passing this to @thomasp85 or @hadley (or both) but after chatting with Thomas I thought I'd make an attempt at expanding the internals chapter. On the one hand I feel quite uncertain in editing this as I'm closer to the target audience for the chapter, so I may have badly misunderstood how the process works. On the other hand, if I have misunderstood something it may be helpful to see where my mental model went wrong?

The main thing I've done is add a running example: at the top of the chapter there are functions that mimic `ggplot_build()` and `ggplot_gtable()` but return a list of objects that include at various intermediate stages. The idea is to try to visually show the reader a single example of how the layer data is being modified by `ggplot_build()` as the process unfolds, and then what the gtable object looks like as it is being put together. 

I'm not even slightly convinced that I've done this in a sensible way, but I do think that some kind of "scaffolding" along these lines would be useful to a user who is starting to make the jump to being a developer. 

(As usual, apologies if there's something amiss with the PR - I'm slowly learning how this all works!)

Dani

title: removes proj4strings and uses EPSG codes only
description:
This solves the problem we were getting in 1d75c6c0026225b9e9c235f7d04bf6a2177d5b31, and closes #191 in the process. 

The internal representation of crs objects in sf has changed as of version 0.9. It looks like `sf::st_crs()` now accepts user input in multiple formats, and the impression I have is that the proj4strings I'd been using are considered legacy (https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/1225). To keep things simple, I've rewritten the text so that we only use numeric EPSG codes in our examples.

title: ggplot2 should be listed in DESCRIPTION
Scales and guides chapters
description:
This is a first pass at splitting the scales chapter. I've based the structure on the comments in #150  and #160, and broken it into a "Scales" chapter and a "Guides: legends and axes" chapter. This division of responsibility is signposted heavily at the start of the scales chapter. 

For the scales chapter, the structure seems to work quite nicely: with all the "guides" content hived off to its own chapter, it's easy to structure most of the scales chapter around the scale types: position, colour, manual and identity. The position and colour scales sections are both subdivided into continuous and discrete (the section on discrete position scales is short and mostly focused on `scale_x_binned`). The writing in this chapter has been partially smoothed but I'd want to edit it one or two more times!

For the guides chapter, the structure seems okay though perhaps not as elegant as scales. It's roughly the same structure as those sections had in the original, though I did move the discussion of date scales into this chapter (the logic here being that the only content in the date scales section pertains to the idiosyncratic `date_breaks` and `date_labels` arguments, and it feels like this belongs with the more general discussion of breaks and labels). I've not edited this chapter very heavily at this point, and I'm not happy with section names, ordering etc. 

My main questions:

- Does this structure work for you? If so I can continue down this path but I think this is a natural point to see if we're in agreement!
- What additional content from the ecosystem should we add? I'm tempted to mention the paletteer package for colour scales. I've made a minimal attempt to refer to hms in the date scales section.
- Is there anything pressing from recent releases that I should mention here? (I'll take a proper look through changelogs etc later, but I suspect you have better intuitions than me on that!) 

As always, this is very much a work in progress. When you have time I'd appreciate a review, but I have no shortage of other things to occupy myself with :grin:

title: Maps and surfaces chapter
description:
This is not ready to merge, but may be worth a quick look as it stands. Following discussion in #158 I've renamed the chapter "maps and surfaces" and organised it around the following structure:

- Surfaces
- Vector maps
    - Drawing vector boundaries
    - Adding point metadata
    - Adding area metadata
- Raster maps
- Simple features maps  

The content in the first three sections is (at present) largely the same as in 2nd ed. 

- I had some difficulties with the "four types of data" framing in 2nd ed, and restructured it as "three common kinds of map data" (vector, raster, sf), to which metadata of different kinds might be added. In one sense it's odd because sf could be thought of as vector data, but it's qualitatively different so I've added it as a distinct section
- In the vector maps section, the "different kinds of metadata" idea is spelled out explicitly using subsections. To keep it concise, the raster maps section takes the same approach as 2nd ed, gives a single example and then refers to other sections
- The `geom_sf` section is obviously a work in progress. At the moment it provides a cursory introduction to the structure of an sf object, hints a little about the "well known text" representation, and then talks briefly about `coord_sf` and map projections. There's one code snippet that mentions `geom_sf_text` but I haven't fleshed that out yet.

Questions:

- Would you prefer a different structure or does this seem about right?
- How deep do you want to dive into sf? At a minimum I'd want to talk about how to add an existing set of point metadata (e.g., `mi_cities`) to a plot, but I'm not certain how far down the sf rabbit hole to go. 
- Anything else to try to work into this chapter? In #158 I considered mentioning `geom_polygon()` now supporting holes, but that might work better in collective geoms? 

No rush on feedback - I have no shortage of jobs to do :grin: and I imagine you're taking some time to enjoy your award at JSM :tada: :cocktail: but whenever you have a moment to take a quick look I'd appreciate it. Probably better to pick up any major issues now before I start trying to dig too far into the details

title: Initial pass at annotations chapter
description:
I've started work on a rethink to the Annotations chapter. It still needs polish (see my comments below), but I think I've has reached the point where you may wish to comment... and suggest a different direction if this approach doesn't seem right to you! 

The structure of the chapter currently has five sections, but I am tentatively thinking I'll collapse it to four:

- **Adding text labels to points** contains most of the old section on text labels, and adds an example of nice labelling using ggrepel (the previous example with directlabel has moved)

- **Building custom annotations** is the old section that was just labelled Annotations, with a slight rewrite to emphasise that the goal here is merely to illustrate how to build your own annotations using the basic geoms, and ends by describing the annotate() helper function

- **Replacing a legend with text** moves the previous example based on directlabel into its own section and adds a second example using ggforce. My logic here was that the directlabel example felt a little different from the other text label ones -- it's not really labelling specific points its highlighting a group of points. I think it works better with this as a separate section, particularly when accompanied with the geom_mark_ellipse() example. (Possibly this section could be renamed... highlighting groups; and the gghighlight example could be moved here???)

- **Reference lines across facets** has the previous example using the diamonds data, just slightly expanded for clarity. At the moment this feels a little orphaned, and I'm wondering if it would be sensible to rename this "Annotation across facets" and maybe give another example? It might work particularly well if I move the first gghighlight example up to the preceding section, and then talk about faceting with gghighlight? 

- **Other annotation tools** I'm not entirely happy with having an "other" to be honest, so I'm tempted to move the gghighlight example and drop the reference to cowplot? I have a suspicion that it will turn out to be worth referencing cowplot in some other section.

The other thing I considered discussing here is patchwork, but I feel like that's something else? It doesn't seem to belong in a chapter on "Annotation" specifically? 

Let me know what you think of this general plan - I can continue tidying or go in a different direction :-)

title: Issue117
description:
Attempts to resolve #117. 

### Comments requiring no changes:

1. Use `head(mpg)` instead of `mpg` on p14 and elsewhere. Comment: Appears to have resolved on its own, because `mpg` is a tibble rather than a vanilla data frame? The only output that looks awkwardly long that I can see is the session information in the colophon to introduction.rmd

7. p96. mpg is not a time series, can't use filter. Comment: presumably the user was accidentally using `stats::filter` here. The code works fine in the current version where `conflicted::conflict_prefer` specifies `dplyr::filter`. No action needed, but there are a few places where this rule is doing some of the work, so it might be a good idea to mention the conflicted package in the "FAQ" chapter?

### Comments with fixes:

3. Issue: p23: Text mentions "car class" but code plots `drv`. Fix: Text fixed to match code.

5. Issue: p46: Axis labels look strange given how nice the rest of the plot is. Fix: add xlab() and ylab() code. Seems easiest given that both commands were introduced earlier.  

6. Issue: Section 3.5.4 is difficult to follow, especially the parts about lines and paths. Fix: I've expanded this section a little, renaming "off-by-one" as "first value". Might be worth looking at my stylistic choices - my writing style defaults to verbose! 

### Comments needing more substantive decisions:

2. Solutions to the exercises? My $0.02 is that it might be worth considering a "solutions to selected exercises" section at the end of the book, depending on how long it ends up being. Including solutions to all exercises might discourage people from doing it themselves, but including some solutions might be helpful for self-directed learning?

4. The quick plots section feels orphaned - expand or drop? My intuition is that "drop" is the better option. A 3rd ed will have quite a lot of new content, and to my mind this doesn't add much to the book. Quick plots aren't the reason most people like ggplot2 :-)

title: Minimal changes to produce passing travis build
description:
This aim here is to allow the ggplot2 book to build cleanly on travis. It still uses `oldbookdown` and makes almost no changes to any R code shown in the book (the only exceptions being those caused by changes to the `USAboundaries` and `scales` packages since publication of the 2nd edition). 

### changes that alter the code (or output) shown to reader

- The back transformation example in position.rmd produces several pages of warnings about `NaN` values. These are now suppressed in the knitr chunk on line 446

- In scales.Rmd there are a couple of cases where the interface to `scales::unit_format()` etc has changed, so the arguments to `scales::unit_format()` and `scales::dollar_format()` are now named explicitly (I think the dollar one may be unnecessary)

- palette names in the `wesanderson` package have changes since second edition to the book. These are all updated now (e.g. Zissou is now Zissou1). 

- The `USAboundaries` package has changed in two respects since ggplot2 2nd ed: it now generates an sf object, and the underlying data is in the `USAboundariesData` package on ropensci. Lines 685-687 of toolbox.rmd make minimal  changes to the R code in the book. 

### changes that manage dependencies etc

- The DESCRIPTION file lists new package dependencies (mostly linked to the dependency on the `sf` package), and travis.yml includes lines for sources, repos and packages needed to build sf on travis.

- The existing source produces odd method dispatch for `select`. Rather than edit the code in the book, I've used `conflicted::conflict_prefer()` to manage this in the common.R script, explicitly preferring `dplyr::select()`. (Ditto for `tidyr::extract()`)

- In the render-tex.R file, I've added a dummy version of the `tex_chapter()` function that mirrors `oldbookdown::tex_chapter()` but now uses `"--top-level-division=chapter"` as an argument to pandoc. (Presumably this will be irrelevant when moving to new bookdown)

-  In ggplot2-book.tex, I've defined commands for `OperatorTok` and `ControlFlowTok`. The inserted commands don't do anything, but the .tex files generated by current version of pandoc now include those

- The common.R script now calls `tools::file_path_sans_ext()` in place of the (now deleted) internal `knitr:::sans_ext()` function.
 
### miscellaneous

- for no particularly good reason the repository is reset to the "clean" state so the generated tex files for each chapter are deleted. 

- travis log for the current build: https://travis-ci.org/djnavarro/ggplot2-book/jobs/545943102

- I'm still learning the etiquette of making a PR. My apologies in advance if something is awry! 

- just in case :-)  "I assign the copyright of this contribution to Hadley Wickham"
